{{Short description|American physical chemist}}
'''Andreas Christoph Albrecht''' (3 June 1927 – 26 September 2002) was an American physical chemist.

== Life ==
Andreas Christoph Albrecht was born in California and raised in [[Washington, D.C.]], [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana|Baton Rouge]] and [[Vienna]]. His father was a German anthropologist.<ref name="JPCAbio">{{Cite journal|last1=Fischer|first1=Peer|last2=Houston|first2=Paul|last3=Loring|first3=Roger|date=2003|title=Biography of Andreas C. Albrecht June 3, 1927−September 26, 2002|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|volume=107|issue=40|pages=8009–8011|doi=10.1021/jp030842v|issn=1089-5639}}</ref> He studied chemistry at [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he met Genia Solomon, who would later become his wife. He completed his studies in 1950. The pair moved to Washington state for graduate school. They both earned doctorates in 1954 from the [[University of Washington]], his in chemistry under W. T. Simpson and hers in biochemistry. Subsequently, Andreas and Genia moved to [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] to work as [[postdoctoral researcher]]s. His postdoctoral supervisor was [[Walter H. Stockmayer]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Genia worked at [[Harvard University]].<ref name="JPCAbio" /><ref name="GeniaObit">{{Cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/name/genia-albrecht-obituary?pid=141071967|title=Genia Solomon Albrecht|last=|first=|date=|website=[[Legacy.com]]|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2020-02-04}}</ref>

In 1956 they moved to [[Ithaca, New York]] so that he could become an instructor at [[Cornell University]]. He was later promoted to Assistant Professor (1957), Associate Professor (1962) and full Professor (1965) of [[physical chemistry]]. Genia paused her scientific pursuits to raise four children. In the 1980s she resumed her career and became a Senior Lecturer in Biochemistry at Cornell where she was honored for her teaching contributions.<ref name="CornChron">{{Cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2010/06/memorial-scheduled-genia-and-andreas-albrecht|title=Memorial slated July 10 to celebrate lives of Genia and Andreas Albrecht|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en|access-date=2020-02-04}}</ref><ref name="GeniaObit" />

==Research==

Albrecht is most well known for his work on the theory of [[Resonance Raman spectroscopy|resonance Raman]] [[Raman scattering|scattering]] intensities.<ref name="JPCAbio" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Albrecht|first=Andreas C.|date=1961|title=On the Theory of Raman Intensities|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|language=en|volume=34|issue=5|pages=1476–1484|doi=10.1063/1.1701032|issn=0021-9606}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Albrecht|first1=A. C.|last2=Hutley|first2=M. C.|date=1971|title=On the Dependence of Vibrational Raman Intensity on the Wavelength of Incident Light|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|language=en|volume=55|issue=9|pages=4438–4443|doi=10.1063/1.1676771|issn=0021-9606}}</ref> He developed two of the main methods for analyzing Raman enhancement patterns. The first of these is the sum-over-states method, developed in the 1960s. After the development of the competing time-dependent [[wavepacket]] method by Lee and [[Eric J. Heller|Heller]], Albrecht's group developed the transform theory of resonance Raman enhancement.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Champion|first1=P M|last2=Albrecht|first2=A C|date=1982-10-01|title=Resonance Raman Scattering: The Multimode Problem and Transform Methods|journal=Annual Review of Physical Chemistry|volume=33|issue=1|pages=353–376|doi=10.1146/annurev.pc.33.100182.002033|issn=0066-426X}}</ref><ref name="McHale">{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Vibrational Spectroscopy|last=McHale|first=Jeanne L.|publisher=Wiley|year=2002|isbn=0471988472|volume=1|location=Chichester|pages=535–556|chapter=Resonance Raman Spectroscopy}}</ref>

Other notable research developments by his group research include [[Thermal blooming|thermal lensing]] spectroscopy,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Long|first1=M. E.|last2=Swofford|first2=R. L.|last3=Albrecht|first3=A. C.|date=1976-01-16|title=Thermal lens technique: a new method of absorption spectroscopy|journal=Science|language=en|volume=191|issue=4223|pages=183–185|doi=10.1126/science.1246605|issn=0036-8075|pmid=1246605}}</ref> and the concept of local molecular vibrational modes.<ref name="JPCAbio" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Swofford|first1=Robert L.|last2=Long|first2=M. E.|last3=Albrecht|first3=A. C.|date=1976-07-01|title=C–H vibrational states of benzene, naphthalene, and anthracene in the visible region by thermal lensing spectroscopy and the local mode model|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|volume=65|issue=1|pages=179–190|doi=10.1063/1.432815|issn=0021-9606}}</ref>

==Awards and achievements==

Andreas Albrecht had many achievements and belonged to many scientific societies. He also had several visiting professorships. In 1986 he was given the New York Academy of Science Polychrome Corporation Award in Photochemistry, in 1988 the [[Lippincott (brand consultancy)|Lippincott]]-Medal and in 1990 the [[Earle K. Plyler]] Prize from the [[American Physical Society]]. In 1992 he joined the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name="JPCAbio" /> A special issue of ''[[The Journal of Physical Chemistry A]]'' was dedicated to him after his death.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ziegler|last2=Fischer|first2=Peer|last3=Korenowski|first3=Jerry|date=2003-10-01|title=A. C. Albrecht Remembrances|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|volume=107|issue=40|pages=8012–8014|doi=10.1021/jp0309116|issn=1089-5639}}</ref>
